summary.text: In fact the denominator divides each convolution summand: for every prime \(p\ne3\), Kummer-style carry counts at each power \(p^i\), combined with a residue inequality accounting for the factor \(2n-1\), show that the summand’s \(p\)-adic valuation is at least that of the denominator. For \(p=3\), the analogous valuation inequality follows from Legendre’s ternary digit-sum formula and the elementary divisibility \(2n-1\mid\binom{2n}{n}\); summing the termwise divisibilities completes the argument.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T(r)=\binom{6r}{3r}\binom{3r}{r}
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(r\). We prove the stronger assertion that, whenever \(n\geq 1\),
\[
(2n-1)\binom{3n}{n}\mid T(k)T(n-k)                 \tag{1}
\]
for every \(0\leq k\leq n\). Summing (1) over \(k\) will immediately prove the required divisibility of the self-convolution.

We write \(v_p(M)\) for the exponent of a prime \(p\) in a positive integer \(M\). We will use two standard valuation descriptions. First,
\[
v_p(M)=\sum_{i\geq1}{\bf1}_{p^i\mid M},             \tag{2}
\]
where \({\bf1}_P\) is \(1\) when \(P\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Second, the carry form of the valuation formula for binomial coefficients says that
\[
v_p\binom{a+b}{a}
 =\sum_{i\geq1}{\bf1}_{p^i\leq (a\bmod p^i)+(b\bmod p^i)}.       \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the summand records whether addition of the residues of \(a\) and \(b\) modulo \(p^i\) produces a carry across the \(p^i\)-place. All sums in (2) and (3) are finite, because their summands vanish once \(p^i\) is larger than the integers involved.

We first establish the elementary modular comparison that will handle all primes other than \(3\).

Fix integers \(q\geq2\), \(k,j\geq0\), with \(k+j\geq1\), and suppose \(q\ne3\). For an integer \(x\), consider the two carry conditions
\[
A_q(x):\quad q\leq (3x\bmod q)+(3x\bmod q),
\]
\[
B_q(x):\quad q\leq (x\bmod q)+(2x\bmod q).
\]
We claim that
\[
\begin{aligned}
&{\bf1}_{q\mid 2(k+j)-1}+{\bf1}_{B_q(k+j)}\\
&\qquad\leq {\bf1}_{A_q(k)}+{\bf1}_{B_q(k)}
             +{\bf1}_{A_q(j)}+{\bf1}_{B_q(j)}.       \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]

We prove this carefully. We need three elementary observations.

First, if neither \(A_q(x)\) nor \(B_q(x)\) holds, then
\[
6(x\bmod q)<q.                                       \tag{5}
\]
To see this, put \(r=x\bmod q\), so \(0\leq r<q\). If \(2r<q\), failure of \(B_q(x)\) gives
\[
r+(2r\bmod q)=3r<q.
\]
Consequently \(3r<q\), so \(3r\bmod q=3r\), and failure of \(A_q(x)\) gives \(6r<q\), as desired.

It remains to see that the alternative \(2r\geq q\) is impossible under the two failures. In that case \(2r\bmod q=2r-q\), and failure of \(B_q(x)\) gives \(3r<2q\). Thus \(q\leq 3r<2q\), so \(3r\bmod q=3r-q\). Failure of \(A_q(x)\) then gives
\[
2(3r-q)<q,
\]
or \(6r<3q\), hence \(2r<q\), contradicting \(2r\geq q\). This proves (5).

Second, either of the conditions
\[
B_q(s),\qquad (2s\bmod q)=1                         \tag{6}
\]
implies
\[
q\leq 3(s\bmod q).                                  \tag{7}
\]
For \(B_q(s)\), put \(r=s\bmod q\). Since \(2s\bmod q=2r\bmod q\leq2r\), the defining inequality for \(B_q(s)\) directly gives \(q\leq3r\). If instead \(2s\bmod q=1\), then \(2r\bmod q=1\). It is impossible that \(2r<q\), since this would say that the even integer \(2r\) equals \(1\). Therefore \(2r\geq q\), and again \(q\leq2r\leq3r\).

Third, when \(q\ne3\), the two conditions in (6) cannot both hold. Indeed, if \(2s\bmod q=1\) and \(B_q(s)\), then, writing \(r=s\bmod q\), the latter condition says \(q\leq r+1\). Since \(r<q\), this forces \(r=q-1\). But then
\[
2s\bmod q=2(q-1)\bmod q=q-2.
\]
For this to equal \(1\), one must have \(q=3\), contrary to the hypothesis.

We now prove (4). Put \(s=k+j\). Since \(s\geq1\),
\[
q\mid 2s-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2s\bmod q=1.             \tag{8}
\]
By the third observation, the two indicators on the left of (4) cannot both be \(1\); hence their sum is at most \(1\).

If both are zero, (4) is immediate. Otherwise, by (7) and (8),
\[
q\leq3(s\bmod q).
\]
Also
\[
s\bmod q=(k+j)\bmod q=((k\bmod q)+(j\bmod q))\bmod q
 \leq (k\bmod q)+(j\bmod q).
\]
It follows that
\[
q\leq3(k\bmod q)+3(j\bmod q).                       \tag{9}
\]
If all four indicators on the right side of (4) were zero, (5), applied first to \(k\) and then to \(j\), would give
\[
6(k\bmod q)<q,
\qquad
6(j\bmod q)<q.
\]
Adding these inequalities yields
\[
3(k\bmod q)+3(j\bmod q)<q,
\]
contradicting (9). Thus at least one right-hand indicator is \(1\). Since the left side is at most \(1\), inequality (4) follows.

We apply (4) to obtain the required valuation inequality for a prime \(p\ne3\). Fix \(0\leq k\leq n\), put \(j=n-k\), so \(k+j=n\), and take \(q=p^i\) for each \(i\geq1\). We have \(q\geq2\). Moreover \(q\ne3\): if \(p^i=3\), then \(p\mid3\), forcing the prime \(p\) to be \(3\).

Using (2) for \(2n-1\) and (3) for the five binomial coefficients, inequality (4), summed over all \(i\geq1\), becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
&v_p(2n-1)+v_p\binom{3n}{n}\\
&\quad\leq v_p\binom{6k}{3k}+v_p\binom{3k}{k}
 +v_p\binom{6j}{3j}+v_p\binom{3j}{j}.                \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, the two terms on the left of (4) respectively count \(p^i\mid2n-1\) and the carry obtained when adding \(n\) and \(2n\), which is the \(i\)-th contribution to \(v_p\binom{3n}{n}\). The four terms on the right count, respectively, the carries in adding \(3k+3k\), \(k+2k\), \(3j+3j\), and \(j+2j\), exactly the four binomial valuations on the right of (10).

It remains to prove (10) for the exceptional prime \(p=3\). We use ternary digit sums. Let \(s_3(m)\) denote the sum of the base-\(3\) digits of \(m\). Legendre's formula gives
\[
2v_3(m!)=m-s_3(m).                                   \tag{11}
\]
Applying (11) to \((a+b)!/(a!b!)\) gives the useful identity
\[
2v_3\binom{a+b}{a}+s_3(a+b)=s_3(a)+s_3(b).           \tag{12}
\]
We will also use
\[
s_3(3m)=s_3(m),                                      \tag{13}
\]
which is immediate because multiplication by \(3\) merely appends a zero ternary digit.

Before carrying out the digit-sum calculation, we need an auxiliary divisibility:
\[
2m+1\mid \binom{2m+2}{m+1}                           \tag{14}
\]
for every \(m\geq0\). First note that
\[
\gcd(2m+1,m+1)=1,
\]
because any common divisor divides
\(2(m+1)-(2m+1)=1\). The standard adjacent-binomial identity gives
\[
(2m+1)\binom{2m}{m}=(m+1)\binom{2m+1}{m+1}.
\]
By symmetry \(\binom{2m+1}{m+1}=\binom{2m+1}{m}\). Since \(2m+1\) is coprime to \(m+1\), it follows that
\[
2m+1\mid\binom{2m+1}{m}.
\]
A second adjacent-binomial identity is
\[
(m+1)\binom{2m+2}{m+1}=(2m+2)\binom{2m+1}{m}.
\]
The right side is divisible by \(2m+1\). Again using coprimality with \(m+1\), we obtain (14).

Taking \(m=n-1\) in (14), valid since \(n\geq1\), gives
\[
2n-1\mid\binom{2n}{n},

def\]
and hence
\[
v_3(2n-1)\leq v_3\binom{2n}{n}.                    \tag{15}
\]
(The stray notation “def” in the displayed line has no mathematical role; the assertion is simply the stated divisibility.)

Now put again \(j=n-k\). Formula (12), followed by (13), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2v_3\binom{6k}{3k}
 &=2s_3(3k)-s_3(6k)
  =2s_3(k)-s_3(2k),\\
2v_3\binom{3k}{k}
 &=s_3(k)+s_3(2k)-s_3(3k)
  =s_3(2k).
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently
\[
2\left(v_3\binom{6k}{3k}+v_3\binom{3k}{k}\right)=2s_3(k).       \tag{16}
\]
The same calculation with \(j\) in place of \(k\) gives
\[
2\left(v_3\binom{6j}{3j}+v_3\binom{3j}{j}\right)=2s_3(j).       \tag{17}
\]
For the binomial coefficient in the denominator, (12) and (13) yield
\[
2v_3\binom{3n}{n}
=s_3(n)+s_3(2n)-s_3(3n)=s_3(2n).                    \tag{18}
\]
Also
\[
2v_3\binom{2n}{n}=2s_3(n)-s_3(2n).                 \tag{19}
\]
Finally, applying (12) to \(k+j=n\) shows
\[
s_3(n)\leq s_3(k)+s_3(j),                           \tag{20}
\]
since the difference on the right is \(2v_3\binom{n}{k}\geq0\).

Combining (15), (18), (19), and (20), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\left(v_3(2n-1)+v_3\binom{3n}{n}\right)
&\leq 2v_3\binom{2n}{n}+2v_3\binom{3n}{n}\\
&=(2s_3(n)-s_3(2n))+s_3(2n)\\
&=2s_3(n)\\
&\leq2s_3(k)+2s_3(j).
\end{aligned}
\]
By (16) and (17), the final quantity is
\[
2\left(
 v_3\binom{6k}{3k}+v_3\binom{3k}{k}
 +v_3\binom{6j}{3j}+v_3\binom{3j}{j}
\right).
\]
Cancelling the factor \(2\) proves (10) for \(p=3\) as well.

Thus, for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p\left((2n-1)\binom{3n}{n}\right)
\leq
v_p\left(
\binom{6k}{3k}\binom{3k}{k}
\binom{6j}{3j}\binom{3j}{j}
\right).
\]
All integers here are positive. Prime factorization therefore implies
\[
(2n-1)\binom{3n}{n}
\mid
\binom{6k}{3k}\binom{3k}{k}
\binom{6j}{3j}\binom{3j}{j}.
\]
With \(j=n-k\), this is exactly the termwise divisibility (1).

It follows that the same denominator divides the sum of these terms:
\[
(2n-1)\binom{3n}{n}
\mid
\sum_{k=0}^{n}
\binom{6k}{3k}\binom{3k}{k}
\binom{6(n-k)}{3(n-k)}\binom{3(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Hence the defining quotient is an integer for every \(n\geq1\).

For \(n=0\), the numerator consists only of the term \(T(0)^2=1\), while
\[
(2\cdot0-1)\binom00=-1.
\]
Thus the quotient equals \(-1\), also an integer. Therefore \(a(n)\) is an integer for every nonnegative integer \(n\).
